t.1.38.1: Śṛṅgin said: Father, whether this was a rash act or whether it was a wicked deed that was done, whether it is pleasing or displeasing to you, the word spoken by me will not be false.
t.1.38.3: I know you, son, to be of fierce power and truthful in speech; no falsehood has ever been spoken by you before, and this will not prove false.
t.1.38.2: This will never be otherwise, father; I tell you so. I do not speak falsely even in idle talk, how much less when uttering a curse?
t.1.38.4: Even when a son has come of age, his father must constantly instruct him, so that he may be endowed with virtues and attain great renown.
t.1.38.5: How much more so in your case, my lord, who are still only a boy, yet empowered by austerity! For the anger of powerful, great-souled beings grows exceedingly.
t.1.38.7: So become endowed with calm, and, gathering the food of the forest, live on, having cast off this anger; thus you will not abandon your dharma.
t.1.38.6: So I see that something must be said to you, O best of those who uphold dharma, considering that you are my son, your childishness, and your rashness.
t.1.38.8: For anger steals away the dharma of ascetics, gathered with hardship; and then, for those bereft of dharma, the desired goal is not to be found.
t.1.38.9: For it is tranquility alone that brings success to forbearing ascetics; this world belongs to the forbearing, and the world beyond as well belongs to the forbearing.
t.1.38.10: Therefore you should always conduct yourself with a forbearing nature, your senses subdued; through forbearance you will attain the worlds that lie next to Brahman's.
t.1.38.12: You have been cursed by my son, a mere boy of unripe understanding, who, O king, could not bear it when he saw this insult done to me by you.
t.1.38.11: But, holding to calm, I will today do what can be done by me now, my son: I will send word to the king.
t.1.38.13: Having thus instructed his disciple, that great ascetic of firm vows, moved by compassion, sent him to King Parikṣit.
t.1.38.14: Having charged his disciple named Gauramukha, a man of good conduct and composed mind, with an inquiry after the king's welfare and also with an account of what had happened,
t.1.38.15: Then he quickly went to the lord of men, the prosperer of the Kurus, and, having first been announced by the doorkeepers, entered the king's palace.
t.1.38.16: Then the brahmin Gauramukha, honored by the lord of men and fully rested, related everything to the king without omission in the presence of the ministers: the dreadful message of Śamīka, just as it had been spoken.
t.1.38.17: O king of kings, there lives in your realm a seer named Śamīka, supremely righteous in spirit, self-controlled, tranquil, and of great austerity.
t.1.38.19: By him you have been cursed, O king of kings, today, without his father's knowledge: within seven nights Takṣaka will indeed be your death.
t.1.38.18: O tiger among men, a serpent deprived of life by you was hung on his shoulder with the tip of your bow, O best of the Bharatas. He forgave that deed of yours, but his son did not forgive it.
t.1.38.20: Then he said again and again, "Arrange protection for yourself there." And that cannot be made otherwise by anyone at all.
t.1.38.21: For he is unable to restrain his son, who is filled with anger; therefore I have been sent, O king, by him, who desires your welfare.
t.1.38.23: And when the king then heard that the excellent sage was keeping a vow of silence, he became all the more tormented in mind with grief.
t.1.38.22: Having heard those terrible words, that king, the joy of the Kurus, a king of great austerity, was tormented with remorse at having committed that evil deed.
t.1.38.25: For the king, resembling an immortal, did not so much regret hearing of his own death as he grieved at having done that deed here.
t.1.38.24: But having come to understand the compassionate nature of that Śamīka, he was tormented all the more, having committed that offense against the sage.
t.1.38.26: Then the king sent that Gauramukha off at that time, saying, "May the blessed one once more show favour to me."
t.1.38.27: And as soon as Gauramukha had departed, the king, his mind deeply agitated, then took counsel together with his ministers.
t.1.38.28: Having taken counsel together with his ministers, he who knew the essence of counsel had a palace built, resting on a single pillar and well guarded.
t.1.38.30: Staying there, guarded on all sides, he, the knower of dharma, carried out all the affairs of kingship together with his ministers.
t.1.38.29: He arranged protection there, and on every side he stationed physicians and medicines, and brāhmaṇas whose mantras were perfected.
t.1.38.31: But when that seventh day had arrived, O best of the twice-born, the learned Kāśyapa came to cure that king.
t.1.38.32: For he had heard that today Takṣaka, the best of serpents, would lead that best of kings to the abode of Yama.
t.1.38.33: Thinking, "Him, bitten by the lord of serpents, I shall free from the fever of the poison; in that there will be both wealth and merit for me,"
t.1.38.34: Takṣaka, the lord of serpents, having become a Brahmin advanced in years, saw that Kāśyapa on the road, going along with single-minded purpose.
t.1.38.35: The lord of serpents said to him, Kāśyapa, the bull among sages: "Where are you going in such haste, and what task do you wish to accomplish?"
t.1.38.36: Kāśyapa said: Today Takṣaka, the foremost of serpents, will burn with his fiery energy King Parikṣit, the tamer of foes, born in the lineage of the Kurus.
t.1.38.37: Gentle one, I am going swiftly to make that king free of fever at once, the perpetuator of the Pāṇḍavas' lineage, of boundless might, who has been bitten by that lord of serpents whose fiery energy equals that of Agni.
t.1.38.38: Takṣaka said: "I am that Takṣaka, O brahmin, and I shall burn that lord of the earth. Turn back, for you are not able to cure one who has been bitten by me."
t.1.38.39: Kāśyapa said: "O Nāga, relying on the power of my knowledge, I shall free that king, bitten by you, from the fever of the poison; such is my resolve."
